title: Flood Fill
summary: Starting from one pixel, repaint it and every connected pixel of the same original colour. DFS spreads in four directions and only continues into cells that still have the original colour.

complexity.note: Each pixel is painted once; recursion can be as deep as the region.

intuition: Pixels of the original colour that touch each other form one region.
Paint a cell before recursing so it isn't visited again.
If the new colour equals the original, return immediately, or the DFS never ends.
pitfalls: Missing the same-colour check: infinite recursion.
Moving diagonally; only 4 directions count.
Forgetting bounds checks before reading `image[r][c]`.

title: Number of Islands
summary: Count groups of connected land cells. Scan the grid; each time you find unvisited land, that's a new island. DFS from it and sink every connected land cell (turn it to water) so it's never counted again.

complexity.note: Each cell is visited a constant number of times; recursion depth can reach m·n.

intuition: An island is a connected component of '1' cells (4-directional).
The outer scan finds a new island each time it hits a '1'.
DFS sinks the whole island, marking it visited in place.
BFS or union-find work equally well.
pitfalls: Counting cells instead of islands.
Using diagonal neighbours.
Very large grids can overflow the recursion stack; BFS avoids that.

title: Clone Graph
category: Graphs · DFS with a visited map
summary: Deep-copy a connected undirected graph. DFS through the original; a map from original node to its copy both prevents infinite loops on cycles and lets each copy link to the copies of its neighbours.

complexity.note: Each node is copied once and each edge followed twice.

intuition: The map `old → copy` doubles as the visited set.
Create the copy before recursing into neighbours, so cycles find it in the map.
Each copy's neighbour list holds copies, never originals.
pitfalls: Recursing before storing the copy in the map loops forever on cycles.
Returning original nodes inside the clone's neighbour lists.
Not handling a null input.

title: Rotting Oranges
summary: Every minute, rotten oranges rot their fresh neighbours. Start a BFS from all rotten oranges at once; each BFS layer is one minute. If fresh oranges remain at the end, return -1.

complexity.note: Each orange enters the queue at most once.

intuition: All initially rotten oranges spread at the same time: put them all in the queue first.
Process the queue level by level; each level is one minute.
Count fresh oranges up front and decrement as they rot.
Fresh oranges left over can't be reached: -1.
pitfalls: Running a separate BFS from each rotten orange gives wrong times.
Counting a minute for the last level even though nothing new rotted.
Returning 0 vs -1 when there are no fresh oranges at all (answer 0).

Python.code:
# DIRS = [(1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)]: down, up, right, left
def orangesRotting(grid: List[List[int]]) -> int:
    m, n = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    queue = deque((r, c) for r in range(m) for c in range(n) if grid[r][c] == 2)
    fresh = sum(row.count(1) for row in grid)
    minutes = 0
    while queue and fresh > 0:
        minutes += 1
        for _ in range(len(queue)):
            r, c = queue.popleft()
            for dr, dc in DIRS:
                nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
                if 0 <= nr < m and 0 <= nc < n and grid[nr][nc] == 1:
                    grid[nr][nc] = 2
                    fresh -= 1
                    queue.append((nr, nc))
    return minutes if fresh == 0 else -1

title: 01 Matrix

intuition: Reverse the question: spread outward from every 0 simultaneously.

pitfalls: Running a BFS from each 1 separately is O((m·n)²).
A two-pass DP (top-left, then bottom-right) also works; know it as an alternative.

title: Surrounded Regions
summary: Capture every 'O' region that is fully surrounded by 'X'. Reverse the problem: any 'O' connected to the border can't be captured. Mark those safe with a DFS from every border 'O', then flip the rest to 'X' and restore the safe ones.

complexity.note: Each cell is visited a constant number of times.

intuition: A region escapes capture only if it touches the border.
DFS from border 'O's and mark them (e.g. '#').
Final pass: 'O' → 'X' (captured), '#' → 'O' (safe).
pitfalls: Trying to detect surrounded regions directly is much harder.
Forgetting the left/right border columns.

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
category: Graphs · Reverse DFS from two oceans
summary: Find cells whose water can flow to both oceans (water flows to equal or lower neighbours). Flip the direction: from each ocean's border, climb to equal or higher neighbours to find everything that drains into it. The answer is the overlap.

complexity.note: Two traversals, each visiting every cell at most once.

intuition: Searching from every cell is O((m·n)²); searching backwards from the oceans is linear.
Pacific touches the top and left edges; Atlantic the bottom and right.
Reverse flow: move to a neighbour only if it's at least as high.
Cells reachable from both searches are the answer.
pitfalls: Using `<` instead of `<=`: equal heights let water flow.
Mixing up which edges belong to which ocean.
